objections.gloss: The use of one's own body as life-support for another is, by default, the body-holder's to grant or withhold — so the burden falls on whoever would compel its continued use, not on the pregnant…
objections.title: The objection challenges the burden's direction. A pregnancy, it says, is not a purely private matter on the order of a haircut or a career change: it involves a developing human life, a second party whose stake is the gravest possible. Given that, the default cannot run in favor of termination-on-request. The presumption must favor continuation — the pregnant person who would end the pregnancy bears the burden of justification, not the party who would see it preserved. To treat "her body, her call" as the starting point is to beg the question against the second party by assuming away its standing before the argument has begun. The right placement of the burden is on the chooser to show why the pregnancy may be ended, not on the objector to show why it may not.

objections.gloss: Responsibility for another's need grounds a duty of aid, not a duty to supply one's body — and gestation is the supply of a body. Grant in full that the pregnant person voluntarily created the…
objections.title: The objection turns on a disanalogy the bodily-sovereignty default is said to ignore. Thomson's hostage was kidnapped — wired to the violinist without lifting a finger — whereas the pregnant person, in the ordinary case, voluntarily performed the very act that brings the dependent into being, knowing pregnancy to be its foreseeable result. One who knowingly undertakes an action that creates a dependent, the objection runs, assumes responsibility for that dependent, and assumed responsibilities ground duties. The fetus, moreover, exists only because of her act and depends on her body alone; she has created not merely a need but an exclusive need, and to walk away is not the mere declining of aid a stranger may decline but the abandonment of a dependent one has made. So the bodily-sovereignty default is defeated for the ordinary case: voluntary responsibility converts what would otherwise be a permissible withdrawal into a forbidden one, and the analogy to refusing a kidney one never undertook to provide simply does not reach her.

objections.gloss: The right does not turn on whether the fetus is a person, because it holds either way — and a claim that holds on both answers to a question does not depend on the question. If the fetus is not a…
objections.title: The objection insists the entire question turns on a single metaphysical fact: the moral status of the fetus. Whether abortion may be chosen, it says, depends wholly on whether the fetus is a person. If it is a person, then ending the pregnancy ends a person's life, and no consideration drawn from the pregnant person's body can convert a homicide into a permissible act — the right collapses into a license to kill. If it is not a person, the right is genuine but empty, a permission opposed by no one and needing no defense. Either way, the objection presses, the personhood question is dispositive, and a defense that will not answer it has skipped the one step on which everything depends. A suite that routes around fetal status, in this telling, has not defended the right; it has changed the subject.
